claims.text: Adding 10–30 vol% SiC to ZrB2 and solid-state sintering at 1600–1700 °C will produce a ZrB2–SiC composite.
The resulting composite will contain SiC distributed at ZrB2 grain boundaries.
SiC at the grain boundaries will impede oxygen diffusion.
SiC at the grain boundaries will impede penetration by molten plating metals.
SiC will form a protective glassy SiO2 layer during oxidation.
SiC addition will inhibit grain growth during lower-temperature sintering.
The proposed mechanisms will improve oxidation resistance at lower sintering temperatures.
The proposed mechanisms will improve molten-metal corrosion durability at lower sintering temperatures.
Grain-growth inhibition will help maintain mechanical integrity.
ZrB2–SiC bodies will have greater oxidation resistance than single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens.
ZrB2–SiC bodies will exhibit lower oxidation-related mass loss than the comparison materials.
ZrB2–SiC bodies will resist corrosion in molten Zn or Al better than single-phase and prior lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens.
The flexural strength of the composite will be comparable to or greater than that of prior lower-temperature ZrB2 bodies.
The density of the composite will be comparable to or greater than that of prior lower-temperature ZrB2 bodies.
The proposed composite is applicable for service in air at temperatures up to 1500 °C.
The proposed composite is applicable in molten plating metal at temperatures up to 800 °C.
The magnitude of oxidation and corrosion improvement depends on SiC content and sintering quality.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifies sintering below 1700 °C, whereas the intervention, preparation conditions, and boundary include 1700 °C.
